blocks.body:
In 1859 Riemann explained how the primes are governed by the zeros of $\zeta(s)$. The zeros that matter are not the easy ones at $-2,-4,-6,\dots$ but the infinitely many zeros in the strip $0<\operatorname{Re}s<1$. The first of them is $\tfrac12+14.134725\ldots\,i$.

Nobody can say exactly where these zeros are; that is the Riemann hypothesis. But we can count them with remarkable precision. The number with imaginary part between $0$ and $T$ is about $\frac{T}{2\pi}\log\frac{T}{2\pi e}$. This lesson proves that formula. It also explains how zeros on the critical line are detected, and records Hardy's theorem that there are infinitely many of them.

blocks.title: Where the zeros can be
blocks.body:
Combine three facts.

1. For $\operatorname{Re}s>1$ the Euler product converges absolutely and has no zero factors, so $\zeta(s)\ne0$.

2. By [[functional-equation]] the completed function $\xi(s)=\tfrac12s(s-1)\pi^{-s/2}\Gamma(s/2)\zeta(s)$ is entire and satisfies $\xi(s)=\xi(1-s)$. If $\operatorname{Re}s<0$, then $\xi(s)=\xi(1-s)\ne0$, because $\operatorname{Re}(1-s)>1$. Since $\zeta(s)=\xi(s)\big/\big(\tfrac12s(s-1)\pi^{-s/2}\Gamma(s/2)\big)$, in this half-plane $\zeta$ vanishes exactly at the poles of $\Gamma(s/2)$. These are the trivial zeros $s=-2,-4,\dots$.

3. $\zeta(1+it)\ne0$ (proved in [[pnt]]), and by the functional equation also $\zeta(it)\ne0$ for $t\ne0$.

So every other zero, a nontrivial zero $\rho=\beta+i\gamma$, lies in the open critical strip $0<\beta<1$. These are exactly the zeros of $\xi$. Since $\zeta$ is real on the real axis, $\zeta(\bar s)=\overline{\zeta(s)}$, so $\bar\rho$ is also a zero. The functional equation adds $1-\rho$ and $1-\bar\rho$. The zeros are therefore symmetric about the real axis and about the critical line $\operatorname{Re}s=\tfrac12$. A zero off the line would come with a mirror partner.

There are no zeros on the real segment $(0,1)$. There $(1-2^{1-\sigma})\zeta(\sigma)=1-2^{-\sigma}+3^{-\sigma}-\cdots>0$, an alternating series with decreasing terms, while $1-2^{1-\sigma}<0$. So $\zeta(\sigma)<0$.

blocks.title: The counting function N(T)
blocks.body:
For $T>0$,
$$N(T)=\#\{\rho=\beta+i\gamma:\ \zeta(\rho)=0,\ 0<\beta<1,\ 0<\gamma\le T\},$$
counted with multiplicity. It counts the nontrivial zeros in the upper half of the strip up to height $T$. By symmetry, the number with $|\gamma|\le T$ is $2N(T)$.

blocks.title: Riemann–von Mangoldt formula
blocks.body:
For $T\ge 3$,
$$N(T)=\frac{T}{2\pi}\log\frac{T}{2\pi}-\frac{T}{2\pi}+\frac78+S(T)+O\Big(\frac1T\Big),\qquad S(T)=O(\log T).$$
Here $S(T)=\frac1\pi\arg\zeta(\tfrac12+iT)$, with the argument defined by continuous variation along the segments from $2$ to $2+iT$ to $\tfrac12+iT$, starting from $\arg\zeta(2)=0$. If $T$ is the ordinate of a zero, take the average of the left and right limits. Since $\frac{T}{2\pi}\log\frac{T}{2\pi}-\frac{T}{2\pi}=\frac{T}{2\pi}\log\frac{T}{2\pi e}$, this gives
$$N(T) = \frac{T}{2\pi}\log\frac{T}{2\pi e} + \frac78 + O(\log T).$$
Riemann stated the main term in 1859; von Mangoldt proved it.

blocks.title: Proof of the main term
blocks.body:
Suppose $T$ is not the ordinate of a zero. We count zeros of the entire function $\xi$ with the argument principle ([[residues]]). Write $\xi(s)=(s-1)\pi^{-s/2}\Gamma(\tfrac s2+1)\zeta(s)$, using $\tfrac s2\Gamma(\tfrac s2)=\Gamma(\tfrac s2+1)$.

Let $R$ be the rectangle with vertices $2,\ 2+iT,\ -1+iT,\ -1$. Inside $R$ the zeros of $\xi$ are exactly the nontrivial zeros with $0<\gamma<T$, since $\xi$ has no zeros on the real segment. So $2\pi N(T)=\Delta_{\partial R}\arg\xi$.

On the bottom edge $\xi$ is real and nonzero, so $\arg\xi$ does not change. The reflection $s\mapsto1-\bar s$ maps the right half of the boundary, the path $L$ from $2$ to $2+iT$ to $\tfrac12+iT$, onto the left half. Since $\xi(1-\bar s)=\overline{\xi(s)}$, the left half contributes the same change of argument as $L$. Therefore
$$\pi N(T)=\Delta_L\arg\xi(s).$$
Now add up the four factors along $L$.

- $s-1$ runs from $1$ to $-\tfrac12+iT$, so its argument changes by $\tfrac\pi2+\arctan\frac1{2T}=\tfrac\pi2+O(1/T)$.
- $\pi^{-s/2}=e^{-\frac s2\log\pi}$ has argument $-\frac t2\log\pi$, which changes by $-\frac T2\log\pi$.
- $\Gamma(\tfrac s2+1)$ is real and positive at $s=2$, so its argument change is $\operatorname{Im}\log\Gamma(\tfrac54+\tfrac{iT}2)$. Stirling's formula $$\log\Gamma(z)=(z-\tfrac12)\log z-z+\tfrac12\log2\pi+O(1/|z|)$$ ([[gamma]]) gives $\frac T2\log\frac T2-\frac T2+\frac{3\pi}8+O(1/T)$.
- $\zeta$ contributes $\pi S(T)$, by definition.

Adding: $$\pi N(T)=\frac T2\log\frac{T}{2\pi}-\frac T2+\frac{7\pi}8+\pi S(T)+O(1/T)$$. Divide by $\pi$.

blocks.title: Proof that S(T) = O(log T)
blocks.body:
On the vertical segment from $2$ to $2+iT$, $\operatorname{Re}\zeta(2+it)\ge1-\sum_{n\ge2}n^{-2}=2-\pi^2/6>0$, so the argument stays in $(-\pi/2,\pi/2)$.

On the horizontal segment from $2+iT$ to $\tfrac12+iT$, between consecutive zeros of $\operatorname{Re}\zeta$ the argument changes by at most $\pi$. So it suffices to show that $\sigma\mapsto\operatorname{Re}\zeta(\sigma+iT)$ has $O(\log T)$ zeros in $[\tfrac12,2]$. Put $f(z)=\tfrac12\big(\zeta(z+iT)+\zeta(z-iT)\big)$, which is holomorphic for $|z-2|\le\tfrac74$ when $T\ge3$. For real $z=\sigma$ we have $f(\sigma)=\operatorname{Re}\zeta(\sigma+iT)$. Also $|f(2)|\ge2-\pi^2/6$.

From $\zeta(s)=\frac{s}{s-1}-s\int_1^\infty\{u\}u^{-s-1}\,du$ one gets $|\zeta(s)|\le C|t|$ for $\operatorname{Re}s\ge\tfrac14$, $|t|\ge1$, so $|f|\le C(T+2)$ on the disc. Jensen's formula bounds the number of zeros of $f$ in $|z-2|\le\tfrac32$, a disc containing $[\tfrac12,2]$, by
$$\frac{\log\big(C(T+2)/(2-\pi^2/6)\big)}{\log(7/6)}=O(\log T).$$

blocks.title: Detecting zeros on the critical line
blocks.body:
Counting zeros is one thing; showing that they lie on $\operatorname{Re}s=\tfrac12$ is another. The tool is a real-valued function. Let $\vartheta(t)$ be the continuous argument of $\pi^{-it/2}\Gamma(\tfrac14+\tfrac{it}2)$ with $\vartheta(0)=0$, and define Hardy's function
$$Z(t)=e^{i\vartheta(t)}\zeta(\tfrac12+it).$$
It is real for real $t$. To see why, note that $F(s)=\pi^{-s/2}\Gamma(s/2)\zeta(s)$ satisfies $F(s)=F(1-s)$ and $F(\bar s)=\overline{F(s)}$, and on the critical line $1-s=\bar s$. So $F(\tfrac12+it)=F(\tfrac12-it)=\overline{F(\tfrac12+it)}$ is real, and $Z(t)$ is $F(\tfrac12+it)$ divided by the positive number $\pi^{-1/4}|\Gamma(\tfrac14+\tfrac{it}2)|$. Also $|Z(t)|=|\zeta(\tfrac12+it)|$.

So every sign change of $Z$ is a zero of $\zeta$ exactly on the critical line, and sign changes can be certified by finite computation. If the number of sign changes up to $T$ equals $N(T)$, all zeros up to height $T$ are on the line and simple. Since $N(T)$ is an integer, it can be computed exactly from the formula above by evaluating $S(T)$ numerically to within $\tfrac12$. Turing's method makes this rigorous. Computations of this kind have verified the Riemann hypothesis up to very large heights.

blocks.title: Hardy's theorem (1914)
blocks.body: Infinitely many nontrivial zeros of $\zeta$ lie on the critical line $\operatorname{Re}s=\tfrac12$.

blocks.title: Beyond Hardy
blocks.body:
We omit the proof of Hardy's theorem. A standard proof compares $\int_T^{2T}Z(t)\,dt$ with $\int_T^{2T}|Z(t)|\,dt$. If $Z$ had constant sign for all large $t$, the two would agree up to sign, but their asymptotic sizes are different.

Later results give positive proportions of all zeros. Selberg (1942) showed that a positive proportion of zeros lie on the line, Levinson (1974) that more than one third do, and Conrey (1989) that more than two fifths do. The Riemann hypothesis asserts that all of them do.

blocks.title: Testing the formula
blocks.body: Compare $N(T)$ with the main term $\frac{T}{2\pi}\log\frac{T}{2\pi e}+\frac78$ for $T=50,100,1000$.
blocks.solution:
The ordinates of the first zeros are $14.1347,\ 21.0220,\ 25.0109,\dots$. Counting them gives $N(50)=10$, $N(100)=29$, $N(1000)=649$.

The main term gives $9.42$ at $T=50$, $29.002$ at $T=100$ and $648.62$ at $T=1000$. The discrepancy is exactly $S(T)$ (up to $O(1/T)$). Here it is small, below $1$ in absolute value, even though the theorem only guarantees $O(\log T)$. This is typical: $S(T)$ grows extremely slowly and is small on average.

blocks.title: Average spacing
blocks.body: How far apart are consecutive zeros near height $T$? Test the prediction on the zeros with $900<\gamma\le1000$.
blocks.solution:
Differentiate the main term: $\frac{d}{dT}\Big(\frac{T}{2\pi}\log\frac{T}{2\pi e}\Big)=\frac1{2\pi}\log\frac{T}{2\pi}$. So near height $T$ there are about $\frac1{2\pi}\log\frac T{2\pi}$ zeros per unit length, and the mean gap is $\frac{2\pi}{\log(T/2\pi)}$. The zeros get denser, but only logarithmically.

Between $900$ and $1000$ the main term predicts $79.87$ zeros; in fact $N(1000)-N(900)=649-569=80$. The mean gap there is about $1.25$. Rescaling the gaps by this mean spacing is the starting point of [[pair-correlation]].

blocks.title: Finding the first zero
blocks.body: Show numerically that $\zeta$ has a zero on the critical line with $14<\gamma<14.3$, and explain why it is the lowest nontrivial zero.
blocks.solution:
Numerically $Z(14)\approx-0.1056$ and $Z(14.3)\approx+0.1328$. Since $Z$ is real and continuous, it vanishes in between, at $14.134725\ldots$. That gives a zero $\tfrac12+14.1347\ldots i$ exactly on the line.

That it is the lowest one does not follow from sign changes alone, since a zero off the line would not show up as a sign change of $Z$. One computes $N(T)$ exactly for some $T$ between $14.14$ and $21$ by the argument principle (numerically, $\Delta\arg\xi$ around the rectangle is $2\pi$). Then $N=1$ there, and the zero already found is the only one. In particular $N(14)=0$.

blocks.title: How large is the sum of 1/|rho|?
blocks.body: Show that $\sum_{0<\gamma\le T}\frac1\gamma=\frac1{4\pi}\log^2T+O(\log T)$. Deduce that $\sum_\rho 1/|\rho|$ diverges, while $\sum_\rho1/|\rho|^{1+\varepsilon}$ converges for every $\varepsilon>0$.
blocks.solution:
Write the sum as a Stieltjes integral and integrate by parts. Since $N(t)=0$ for $t<14$,
$$\sum_{0<\gamma\le T}\frac1\gamma=\int_{1}^{T}\frac{dN(t)}{t}=\frac{N(T)}T+\int_1^T\frac{N(t)}{t^2}\,dt .$$
The first term is $O(\log T)$. In the integral insert $N(t)=\frac{t}{2\pi}\big(\log\frac t{2\pi}-1\big)+O(\log(t+2))$, valid for all $t\ge1$:
$$\int_1^T\frac{\log t-\log2\pi-1}{2\pi t}\,dt+O\Big(\int_1^T\frac{\log(t+2)}{t^2}dt\Big)=\frac{\log^2T}{4\pi}+O(\log T).$$
Since $|\rho|\ge\gamma$ and $|\rho|\le\gamma+1$, the sum of $1/|\rho|$ over zeros up to height $T$ is also $\frac{1}{4\pi}\log^2T+O(\log T)$, which is unbounded. The same integration by parts with $t^{-1-\varepsilon}$ gives $\int^\infty t^{-2-\varepsilon}\cdot t\log t\,dt<\infty$, so $\sum1/|\rho|^{1+\varepsilon}$ converges. This is why the sum over zeros in the [[explicit-formula]] converges only conditionally.

blocks.body:
- $N(T)$ counts only zeros with $\gamma>0$, and counts them with multiplicity. All zeros computed so far are simple, but that is not proved.
- The $\frac78$ is meaningful only together with $S(T)$. Since $S(T)$ is only known to be $O(\log T)$, the formula as usually quoted, with error $O(\log T)$, cannot see the constant. Littlewood proved $\int_0^TS(t)\,dt=O(\log T)$, so on average the constant is visible.
- Trivial zeros are not counted, and none of them lies in the critical strip.
- Sign changes of $Z(t)$ find zeros on the line, but cannot by themselves rule out zeros off the line. For that one compares with $N(T)$.
- $\log$ is natural, and the main term is $\frac{T}{2\pi}\log\frac{T}{2\pi e}$, not $\frac{T}{2\pi}\log T$. The two differ by about $\frac{T}{2\pi}\log 2\pi e$, a linear amount.

Each zero contributes a term $-x^\rho/\rho$ to $\psi(x)$ in the [[explicit-formula]], and $N(T)$ tells us how many terms there are up to height $T$. Bounds like $\sum_{|\gamma|\le T}1/|\rho|\ll\log^2T$ come straight from it. Normalising the spacing by $\frac{1}{2\pi}\log\frac{T}{2\pi}$ leads to Montgomery's [[pair-correlation]] conjecture and the link with random matrices. Counting zeros with $\beta>\sigma$, rather than all zeros, is the subject of [[zero-density]] estimates. The conjecture that all of them have $\beta=\tfrac12$ is the [[rh]]. Under it, Littlewood improved the bound for $S(T)$ to $O(\log T/\log\log T)$. The growth of $\zeta$ on the line, which controls $S(T)$, is the topic of [[lindelof]].

1. Show that $N(T+1)-N(T)=O(\log T)$: there are only logarithmically many zeros in any window of height $1$.
2. Prove that zeros off the critical line come in groups of four, $\rho,\bar\rho,1-\rho,1-\bar\rho$, and that zeros on the line come in pairs.
3. Using a computer, evaluate $Z(t)$ on a grid in $[14,40]$, locate its sign changes, and compare the count with $N(40)$ from the formula.
4. Show that $\sum_\rho\frac1{|\rho|^2}<\infty$ and compute the order of magnitude of $\sum_{\gamma>T}\frac1{\gamma^2}$.

sources.ref: Titchmarsh, The Theory of the Riemann Zeta-Function (2nd ed., revised by Heath-Brown)
